 4   and Black Anthem Limited (“Black Anthem”) (collectively, “Plaintiffs”), and Defendant, by and

 5   through their respective counsel of record, stipulate as follows:

 6             WHEREAS, counsel for the parties from Keker, Van Nest & Peters LLP, Cahill Gordon

 7   & Reindel LLP, and Quinn Emanuel Urquhart & Sullivan, LLP met and conferred by email and

 8   video conference on August 25, 2026, and in person at the offices of Keker, Van Nest and Peters

10   regarding which of Plaintiffs’ claims are subject to arbitration and which should remain before

11   this Court and to prepare the chart regarding the same that the Court directed the parties to

12   submit;

13             WHEREAS, the parties were in the process of meeting and conferring regarding the chart

14   that the Court directed the parties to submit;

15             WHEREAS, on Wednesday, August 26, 2026, between the parties’ two meet-and-confer

16   sessions, Defendant’s counsel notified Plaintiffs’ counsel for the first time that, based on the

17   citizenship of at least one of its members, Defendant may be, and may have been on the date the

18   Complaint was filed, a foreign citizen (specifically, a citizen of the United Arab Emirates),

19   information which Defendant’s counsel represented it had only recently learned from its client,

20   and which Defendant disclosed to the Court in a Supplemental Disclosure filed on August 26,

21   2026, see Dkt. 66;

22             WHEREAS, the parties discussed that the new information that Defendant may be a

23   citizen of the United Arab Emirates may raise a threshold issue regarding this Court’s subject

24   matter jurisdiction, specifically whether the citizenship of Defendant defeats complete diversity

25   between the parties; and

26             WHEREAS, while the parties understood and were in the process of complying with the

27   Court’s direction at the August 20, 2026, hearing to address their dispute regarding which claims

28   are subject to arbitration and which claims should remain before this Court, in light of the new

 6   meets the high bar for sealing before this Court. World Liberty’s attempt is part of its ongoing

 7   campaign to shield this case—which exposes World Liberty’s misconduct—from the public’s view.

10   referred to one contract that contains a confidentiality provision. (ECF No. 1). That provision was

17   contain any confidentiality provisions and that Plaintiffs have never understood to be confidential:

18   the November 25, 2024 Token Purchase Agreement (“TPA”) by which Plaintiffs acquired two

19   billion of the digital tokens at the center of this case for $30 million (ECF No. 43-5), and an Advisor

23   this case. Indeed, the Complaint mentions the TPA more than 50 times and quotes it liberally

24   throughout. World Liberty’s insistence that the TPA and ATA contain confidential material has no

25   merit. World Liberty could have insisted on confidentiality clauses in them, and it could have asked

26   for those agreements to be redacted at the outset of this case. World Liberty did neither. Moreover,
